title: Measurement of Nontariff Barriers
abstract: As tariffs on imports of manufactures have been reduced as a result of multi-lateral trade negotiations, interest in the extent to which existing nontariff barriers may distort and restrict international trade is growing. Accurate and reliable measures are needed in order to address the issues involving the use and impacts of nontariff barriers. This study assesses currently available methods for quantifying such barriers and makes recommendations as to those methods that can be most effectively employed. The authors focus both on the conceptual issues arising in the measurement of the different types of nontariff barriers and on the applied research that has been carried out in studies prepared by country members of the OECD Pilot Group and others seeking to quantify the barriers. Nontariff barriers include quotas, variable levies, voluntary export restraints, government procurement regulations, domestic subsidies, and antidumping and countervailing duty measures. The authors discuss the many different methods available for measuring the effects of these and other nontariff barriers. Illustrative results are presented for industrial OECD countries, including Australia, Canada, Germany, Norway, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Finally, the authors offer guideline principles and recommend procedures for measuring different types of nontariff barriers. Economists, political scientists, government officials, and lawyers involved in international trade will find this an invaluable resource for understanding and measuring NTBs. Alan V. Deardorff and Robert M. Stern are Professors of Economics and Public Policy, University of Michigan.

Full narrative

Measurement of Nontariff Barriers by Alan Deardorff and Robert Stern was published by University of Michigan Press in 1998. It is part of the Studies in International Economics series. Conceptually, the work connects to Technical barriers to trade, Subsidy, Government procurement, European union and International trade.

OpenAlex records 164 citations. That places it in the top 10% of works in its field and year of publication. Citations peaked in 2009 with 27 citing works. Notable citing venues include SSRN Electronic Journal, RePEc: Research Papers in Economics and AgEcon Search (University of Minnesota, USA). The citing works include 90 journal articles, 26 book chapters, 22 preprints and 6 dissertations. They come from 37 countries, led by the United States, France and China.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This book has become a reference point for scholarship on non-tariff barriers in international trade. With 164 OpenAlex citations and a standing in the top 10% of cited works for its field and year, it shows clear and sustained academic uptake, especially in research on technical barriers to trade, WTO-related policy, and trade regulation.

Full narrative

Published by the University of Michigan Press in 1998 as part of the Studies in International Economics series, Measurement of Nontariff Barriers addresses a policy problem that grew in importance as tariffs declined: how to identify, measure, and compare the trade effects of non-tariff measures. The book’s central contribution is methodological. Rather than treating non-tariff barriers as a single, easily observed category, it evaluates available approaches for quantifying them and offers guidance on which methods are most useful for analysis and policy design.

The citation record suggests that this framing has remained influential over time. The book is cited across a broad set of economics and trade-related venues, including journal articles, book chapters, preprints, reference entries, and reports. The surrounding subject profile is especially strong in global trade and economics, World Trade Organization law, and global trade competitiveness, indicating that the book continues to inform work on trade policy instruments, regulatory obstacles, and market access.

Recent citing works show that the book’s ideas still resonate in current research on technical barriers to trade, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, regulatory distance, and protectionism. That pattern points to durable methodological relevance: scholars are still drawing on the book when they need to operationalize complex policy constraints that do not appear as tariffs but can nonetheless shape trade flows. The citing landscape is international, with uptake visible across multiple countries and institutions, and it includes use in education, government, and nonprofit settings.

There is also some evidence of broader policy relevance. The book aligns with the Sustainable Development Goal on Partnerships for the Goals, which fits its focus on trade rules, negotiation, and international coordination. OpenAIRE records indicate at least one open instance, while the work otherwise appears as a closed book in the repository record. Public-event data are unavailable in the archive, so the record is best understood as showing scholarly and policy uptake rather than documented public-facing discourse.
